title: Things Fall Apart
objective: After this level you can explain how Chinua Achebe wrote back against colonial stories about Africa.
summary: Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958) tells an Igbo story from the inside, in English peppered with Igbo proverbs, to answer colonial novels that cast Africa's past as savagery.

cards.headline: A novel ends with an official planning a book. Its hero gets a paragraph.
cards.body: On the last page of Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart, the District Commissioner decides Okonkwo's story might fill a paragraph in his planned book, The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger. Achebe had just given Okonkwo an entire novel. That gap is the point.

cards.headline: Inside an Igbo village
cards.body: Things Fall Apart, written in English and published in 1958, follows Okonkwo, a leader of an Igbo community, as white missionaries and colonial government intrude in the 1890s. It is traditionally structured and peppered with Igbo proverbs, and it traces the falling apart of Okonkwo and of his village at the same time. You see the world before you see it break.

cards.headline: Why Achebe wrote it
cards.body: Achebe resented the stereotype of Africa as a primitive land, a "heart of darkness," and novels like Joyce Cary's Mister Johnson, with its comic African who adores his white boss. In his essay "The Novelist as Teacher", he said he'd be satisfied if his novels about the past taught readers one thing: their past, imperfect as it was, had not been an age of savagery from which Europeans rescued them.

mascot.line: Keep this: Achebe wasn't only telling a story. He was correcting one that others had told.

cards.headline: A title from Yeats
cards.body: Achebe took his title from W. B. Yeats's poem "The Second Coming": "Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold;". An Igbo story, told in English under an Irish poet's line, answers the colonial novel in its own language. Britannica credits the book with helping create the Nigerian literary renaissance of the 1960s.

questions.prompt: Match each name with what goes with it.

pairs.right: A leader of an Igbo community

questions.explanation: Okonkwo is a leader of an Igbo community. Joyce Cary wrote Mister Johnson, and Achebe's title comes from W. B. Yeats's poem "The Second Coming".

questions.prompt: A new novel retells a colonial war from inside a village that old histories called primitive. Which of Achebe's aims does it share?

options.label: Keeping the colonial official's account as the true record
Showing the people's past was not an age of savagery
Refusing to write in any European language
Retelling Homer's Odyssey in an African setting

questions.explanation: Achebe wanted his novels to show readers their past had not been an age of savagery from which Europeans rescued them, and he told it from the inside.

questions.prompt: Things Fall Apart is peppered with Igbo proverbs, wisdom passed on by voice. Level 1 calls literature kept alive that way _____.

options.label: a fable
options.rationale: A fable is a short tale with a moral, often with animals.

options.label: a modernist fragment
options.rationale: That's a way of building a poem.

options.label: an epic
options.rationale: An epic is a long poem of heroic deeds.

questions.explanation: Level 1 says literature isn't only written: scholars also speak of oral literature, passed on by voice. Achebe carries some of it into the novel.
